entries.section: 1. Enjoying the experience of the resurrection:

paragraphs.text: 1 And he said unto me, Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.

When the prophet beheld the fiery chariot, he fell upon his face in complete helplessness, as though he had reached death. Therefore the Lord commanded him: "Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee" [1]. For one cannot speak with someone who has reached death; rather, it is fitting that he first rise, to enjoy listening to the voice of the Lord. If the mission of God's servants is to bring souls dead in sins into the life of resurrection, then it is all the more fitting for the servants themselves to experience the resurrection within them. This is what happened with Saul of Tarsus, who thought that he was able by himself, by his human zeal, his training in the Law, his personal abilities and his gifts, to serve God; but when he met the Lord Christ he fell to the ground as one dead and realized that he was nothing... Then he heard the divine voice: "Rise, and stand upon thy feet: for I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness both of these things which thou hast seen, and of those things in the which I will appear unto thee" (Acts 26:16). So he arose and enjoyed the new life of resurrection; therefore he preached to the Gentiles "Jesus, and the resurrection" (Acts 17:18). This is the message of the disciples and the Apostles, that "with great power gave the apostles witness of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 4:33).

Moreover, the command given to the prophet to rise and stand upon his feet carries an indication of the necessity of working without ceasing, for God does not work in the slack but in those who strive continually. For by constant work we bear a divine mark, as the Lord Himself said: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work" (Jn 5:17).

The command was given to him to stand upon his feet, fully prepared, to accomplish a holy and weighty mission. He had been deprived of the priestly work because of the captivity, but God calls him to the prophetic work, to present the divine will to a rebellious people. Let him stand in reverent awe before God, listening to His voice with all attention in order to fulfill His will.

entries.section: 2. Working by the Spirit of God:

paragraphs.text: 2 And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me.

The command to rise was given, but how can fallen clay rise?! It needs the Spirit of God Himself, the Giver of life, who grants us union with Christ Jesus who rose from the dead, so that we may experience the power of His resurrection in us.

The prophet Ezekiel describes his resurrection thus: "And the spirit entered into me when he spake unto me, and set me upon my feet, that I heard him that spake unto me" [2]. It is as though he could not hear the divine voice speaking with him, nor enter with Him into the conversation of love, except by the entry of the Holy Spirit into his life. By this he understands the divine words, experiences the divine work, and is able to preach and proclaim by the power of the Spirit!

The prophet Ezekiel began his ministry with the opening of heaven before him, to see the awesome divine chariot; he fell trembling, and needed the Spirit of God to raise him so that he might walk on his feet. As for the Lord Christ, He began His ministry with the opening of heaven, so that those present might realize that He is the only beloved Son of the Father, and behold the Holy Spirit of God resting upon Him in the form of a dove. He opens heaven in order to grant His believers sonship to God, so that they may find a place in the Father's bosom, and receive the Spirit of adoption. The prophet Ezekiel was terrified because through the heavenly chariot he receives the prophecy concerning the divine chastisements, whereas the Lord Christ rejoiced because by His baptism He proclaims the forgiveness of sins and the enjoyment of the believers in the New Covenant of the merits of His precious blood.

entries.section: 3. The sense of stewardship:

paragraphs.text: 3 And he said unto me, Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. 4 For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them; and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD. 5 And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them.

If the work of the Holy Spirit in the life of believers in general is to bring them into the resurrection of the Lord Christ, so that in Baptism they receive the new life in the image of their Creator, then the same Spirit works in the servants of the Church, that they may go down to where people lie in the death of sin, and lead them to the joyful proclamation of their resurrection with Christ and their enjoyment of the risen life. This is the work of the servant... It is a work above all human capacity, it is the work of God Himself, and the servant is only a steward of the mysteries of God. This is what the Lord affirmed, saying: "Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation that hath rebelled against me: they and their fathers have transgressed against me, even unto this very day. For they are impudent children and stiffhearted. I do send thee unto them" [3-4].

It is as though God confirms to him the difficulty of the work: the matter requires going down to rebellious people, impudent and stiffhearted from father to grandfather. Who then will lead them to obedience instead of rebellion, to gentleness instead of harshness, and to an open heart instead of its hardness and closedness?! It is the work of God Himself; therefore He affirms more than once, "I do send thee unto them." It is My mission and not yours, that I work in the heart within, create it anew and grant it life!

This is what all who labor faithfully in the Lord's vineyard have realized. The Apostle Paul says: "Let a man so account of us, as of the ministers of Christ, and stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Cor 4:1). He realized that he is merely a steward who speaks and works not in his own name but in the name of the one who appointed him. St. John Chrysostom comments on this saying thus: [The steward manages the affairs of his master well without attributing to himself what belongs to his master; on the contrary, he attributes what he has to his lord... Do you want an example of faithful stewards? Hear what Peter says: Why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk? (Acts 3:12). And with Cornelius also he said: "Stand up; I myself also am a man." ... And Paul is no less faithful in his saying: "I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Cor 15:10)... And when the Apostle opposed those unfaithful persons he said: "And what hast thou that thou didst not receive?" (1 Cor 4:7)].

The servant, as a steward, works on behalf of his master and not on behalf of himself. Therefore St. John Chrysostom was always wary of the love of vainglory and praise, lest he be usurping the right of God Himself. In this he says: "Surely the mystery of the priesthood will condemn us if we do not use it well," and he also says: [He who enters the work of preaching with such desires (love of praise), what pains and hardships pursue him! It is easier for the sea to be without waves than for such a person to be without troubles or sorrows]. The saint feared for himself as Patriarch of Constantinople, so he said: [I shed tears when I see myself on a throne above the thrones of others, and when more honor is offered to me than to others].

It is not the work of Christ's ambassadors to offer eloquent human phrases, nor to display their achievements and glorify their personal efforts, but to proclaim the word of the Lord Himself, and to call to repentance in a spirit of meekness and humility. The word of the Lord is strong and able, for "where the word of a king is, there is power" (Eccl 8:4), and God is the King of kings; His word shall not return void, without fruit (Isa 55:11).

entries.section: 3. The sense of stewardship:

paragraphs.text: The sense of stewardship gives the servant strength, so that he does not fear the work however difficult or seemingly impossible, working leaning on the breast of the One who appointed him, whatever the results may be, as he hears the divine voice: "I do send thee unto them... And they, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear, (for they are a rebellious house,) yet shall know that there hath been a prophet among them" [5]. This does not mean that God does not know whether they will hear or disobey, but He speaks thus in order to leave them the freedom of obedience or disobedience, so that they will have no excuse that He judged them with disobedience beforehand. As St. John Chrysostom says: [He did not say this out of ignorance, but lest any of the obstinate say that his prophecy bound them to disobedience].

entries.section: 4. Serving with courage:

paragraphs.text: 6 And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, though briers and thorns be with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions: be not afraid of their words, nor be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. 7 And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious.
"And thou, son of man, be not afraid of them, neither be afraid of their words, for they are briers (brambles)
and thorns (prickles) with thee, and thou dost dwell among scorpions. Be not afraid of their words, nor be afraid of their looks.
Be not dismayed, for they are a rebellious house" [6].

The divine mission is not easy, for the servant works as though in the midst of brambles and surrounded by thorns that spoil God's tillage, and like one who dwells among scorpions he is exposed to hidden stings. Yet he must not fear people, nor be troubled by their words or their faces, but, as God had previously commanded Joshua the son of Nun thus:
"Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest" (Josh 1:9).

Indeed, God warned the prophet Jeremiah against fear, saying to him: "Arise, and speak unto them all that I command thee: be not dismayed at their faces, lest I confound thee before them. For, behold, I have made thee this day a defenced city, and an iron pillar, and brasen walls against the whole land... And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the LORD, to deliver thee" (Jer 1:17-19). It is as though God threatens His servant that if he is dismayed, not only will He not protect him, but He Himself will terrify him, for He does not work in the heart that does not lean on Him.

St. John Chrysostom has presented to us a wonderful example of a father filled with tenderness, so that he loved his people more than the light of his eyes; if one of his children fell into sin, he felt within himself as though he were in great danger, like one in a dark prison, or one sentenced to ten thousand lashes, or confined in a deep pit. Therefore he used to cry out to his children, saying: [I can no longer bear more than this! Stretch out your hands toward me and rescue me]. And yet he was frank and courageous, speaking boldly and with power, without fear, saying: [I am ready to bear everything. Whoever persists in his conduct and does not listen to my warning, I will bar from entering the church as with the sound of a trumpet, even if he is a prince or an emperor. How can I sit on this chair if I do not do what befits it?! It is better for me to step down from it, for there is nothing more bitter than a bishop who is of no benefit to his people].

God called the rebellious people brambles, thorns and scorpions, not that the servant should despair of them or despise them, but that he may know the difficulty of the work and prepare for it, and say with righteous Job: "I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls" (Job 30:29), remembering the words of the Apostle: "That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world" (Phil 2:15).

Some may object, saying: Why did the Lord call them thus? St. Clement of Alexandria answers: [This is a very great proof of His love, for despite His perfect knowledge of the shameful state to which the people had come, so that He drove them out and uprooted them (from Jerusalem), He urges them to repentance].

God speaks with all frankness with His servants, declaring to them the difficulty of their mission, for in every generation they find those who resist the truth; and they must prepare to endure pain and persecution, realizing that God grants them grace to be strong to face the opposing currents, so that the servant may know that the path of service is not strewn with roses, but is the narrow way of the cross, which inevitably ends with the joy of the resurrection. Our God has not deceived us, but He reveals to us plainly the difficulty and distress of the way.

entries.section: 4. Serving with courage:

paragraphs.text: God says: "And thou shalt speak my words unto them, whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear: for they are most rebellious" [7]. It is as though his mission is poured into presenting the word of God as it is; they may hear and repent, or they may refrain from responding to the divine voice... So be it. For the success of the servant lies in his faithfulness in presenting the word of the Lord as it is, that is, being faithful in the divine deposit.

entries.section: 5. Attention to his own life:

paragraphs.text: 8 But thou, son of man, hear what I say unto thee; Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house.

Although God chose him for the prophetic work and knows his heart and his striving, yet He warns him, saying: "Be not thou rebellious like that rebellious house" [8]. He feared for him lest, while he preaches obedience to the people, he himself fall with them into rebellion instead of raising them up. It is as though God wanted to affirm to His servant that he should not forget the salvation of his soul and his spiritual life during his service, because many have lost their peace and their salvation during their human zeal and their labor in service. For this reason the Apostle Paul says: "I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway" (1 Cor 9:27). This is what moved St. John Chrysostom, whose heart melted with love for the sake of service, to be watchful not only for the salvation of his brethren but also for the salvation of his own soul, saying: [My words are of more benefit to my own life than to those who hear me], and he also says: [I know the seriousness of this office and the difficulty of its work, and the violent storms that sweep over the soul of the priest, for they are more severe in their turbulence than the storms of the sea].

entries.section: 6. Enjoying the experience of the word of God:

paragraphs.text: 8 open thy mouth, and eat that I give thee. 9 And when I looked, behold, an hand was sent unto me; and, lo, a roll of a book was therein; 10 And he spread it before me; and it was written within and without: and there was written therein lamentations, and mourning, and woe. [8-10].

The subject of his work is "the word of God," which the servant must eat, so that his inner depths are filled with it, and it becomes the subject of his continual thought, and he even hides in it, so that he presents nothing of himself but presents what belongs to God.

Eating the word means its entering into his depths; it turns in his life into blood that flows in his veins. It is as though he is blended with it, and counts it as his life! He eats it and lives by it in order to present it to others by presenting his evangelical life as an epistle read of all men.

St. John Chrysostom was accustomed to present to his people from the table of the Holy Bible almost every day, giving special attention to the Gospel and apostolic word. In one of his homilies he says:
[You have heard the apostolic voice!
It is a heavenly trumpet! It is the harp of the Spirit!
Yes. The reading of the Holy Scriptures is a garden, indeed, it is a paradise also, which offers not only fragrant flowers but also fruits that can nourish the soul...!

We are like men who smelt gold extracted from the apostolic mines, not by throwing it into a furnace, but by depositing it in the minds of your souls, not by kindling an earthly fire but by the inflaming of the Spirit.
So let us gather from it small pieces with diligence and effort... for pearls are not valued according to their size but according to the beauty of their nature].

He received a book written without and within. Perhaps he meant that the word of God is declared outwardly in letters on paper, but the matter needs the work of the Holy Spirit, who reveals in the heart the writing that is within, that is, the deep inner meaning. Perhaps he also meant that this book contains on the outside the sins of the people and their transgressions, while within it carries God's chastisements for their repentance.

entries.section: 6. Enjoying the experience of the word of God:

paragraphs.text: As for the writing, as it came in the Septuagint: "lamentations, and a song, and woe" [10]; the following are some comments of the Fathers on this phrase:
*The whole book is full of woe for the perishing, a song for the saved, and lamentations for those between the two (that is, those on the path of repentance).

Origen * It contains two sorrowful things and one joyful; for whoever weeps much in this time will be saved in the future, because "the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth" (Eccl 7:4), and as the Lord Himself says: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21).

St. Ambrose * Written in it are lamentations, a song and woe. The first of these three concerns you if, as a sinner, you repent of your sins; the second concerns the saints who are called to sing, praising God, because praise is not in the mouth of sinners; and the third concerns those who are in despair like you and have given themselves over to uncleanness, fornication, gluttony and base lusts, people who think that death is the end of everything, and that after death there is nothing else, who say: "When the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us" (Isa 28:15).
The book that the prophet eats is the whole collection of the Holy Scriptures, which makes the penitent lament, the righteous honored, and gives woe to the despairing.
St. Jerome
I long to work in Your vineyard
*You revealed Your heavens to Ezekiel Your prophet, and he longed to serve You; reveal them to me, and I will work earnestly in Your vineyard.

Your heavens are joyful and delightful; working with You is a heavy cross, yet it is exceedingly joyful and delightful. How sweet it is to work with You, for You reveal Yourself to those who work for You and with You.

*You sent Your prophet to a very stubborn people, but Your Spirit raised him that he might raise many. Grant me the Spirit of resurrection, so that I do not fear death. Death has crept into me and into my brethren, but You are the very Resurrection. You sent him to a stubborn people, and feared lest stubbornness seep into him.
Keep me lest in my service I grow weak and fall. Keep me by Your grace and keep Your people.
*What shall I offer to my brethren:

Here I open my mouth for You to stretch out Your hand with the scroll; I eat it and find it sweet, O sweetness of my soul. This outstretched hand is none other than Your incarnation and becoming man; You gave me Your body, O Word, that I may partake of it.
*Your word has sweetness and bitterness:
Make it sweet by Your grace, as I acquire Your divine promises.
Grant me to accept Your chastisements as a temporary bitterness for the correction of my soul and its edification forever.

entries.section: 1. The sweetness of the word of God:

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, eat that thou findest; eat this roll, and go speak unto the house of Israel. 2 So I opened my mouth, and he caused me to eat that roll. 3 And he said unto me, Son of man, cause thy belly to eat, and fill thy bowels with this roll that I give thee. Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness.

The command was given to the prophet Ezekiel to eat the scroll (the word of God), as it was given to St. John the Beloved (Rev 10:9). Jeremiah says: "Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart" (Jer 15:16), and the Lord Christ says: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4). The word of God is a delicious food, giving life and inner joy and gladness; we are nourished by it, and so we carry it in our depths. It is sweet, even if it carries bitterness because of God's chastisements, which are for our salvation.

When the prophet Ezekiel received His word from the hands of God as an open scroll, he read what was inside it and what was outside, and found that it contained lamentations and woe together with songs of praise; so he opened his mouth for God to feed him with His own hand, and his depths were satisfied, and he found it in his mouth as honey for sweetness.

How wonderful is the love of God! He deals with us as a nurse or a tender mother, stretching out His hand to feed us, the infants beloved to Him. We throw ourselves upon His breast like a nursing child on the breast of its mother, and we find His commandment pure milk coming from His breasts (the two Testaments), like the honey of bees and the honeycomb. His commandment is suitable for the little ones and for the mature grown.

God's commandment is hard and heavy for the natural man; indeed, some sometimes see it as a fetter on human freedom. But when the hand of God is stretched out to present it to us within us, we find it sweet as honey. What is this outstretched hand (Ezek 1:9) that Ezekiel saw but the Son of God, who is called "the arm of the Lord," and who became visible through the divine Incarnation? He presented to us the divine commandment not through commands and prohibitions, but through practical mutual love between God and man, and between man and his brother, offering Himself as an example and helper, for He says: "This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you. Ye are my friends... Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you" (Jn 14:12-15). Thus the divine commandment became not an order we are bound to obey, but the opening of our inner insight by love to perceive the will of our Beloved, so that we obey Him as beloved ones whose will meets His divine will voluntarily! By this we can understand His words: "Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me... For my yoke is easy (pleasant), and my burden is light" (Mt 11:29-30), although He had previously said: "Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword... And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:34, 38). By love pain becomes sweet and the cross becomes glory, and the commandment is sweet as honey.

The word of God also carries warnings against the fallen, that they may repent; these put the servant of the word in a difficult position and even expose him to troubles and afflictions, yet at the same time they offer sweetness and joy to the servant, as he realizes God's saving purposes. When the Apostle Paul wrote sternly he grieved the Corinthians, but he went on to explain to them that although they had been grieved, he rejoices in this grief which is unto repentance, so that they too rejoice with him, saying: "For if I make you sorry, who is he then that maketh me glad, but the same which is made sorry by me? And I wrote this same unto you, lest, when I came, I should have sorrow from them of whom I ought to rejoice; having confidence in you all, that my joy is the joy of you all. For out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote unto you with many tears; not that ye should be grieved, but that ye might know the love which I have more abundantly unto you" (2 Cor 2:2-4).

entries.section: 2. The difficulty of the work:

paragraphs.text: 4 And he said unto me, Son of man, go, get thee unto the house of Israel, and speak with my words unto them. 5 For thou art not sent to a people of a strange speech and of an hard language, but to the house of Israel; 6 Not to many people of a strange speech and of an hard language, whose words thou canst not understand. Surely, had I sent thee to them, they would have hearkened unto thee. 7 But the house of Israel will not hearken unto thee; for they will not hearken unto me: for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted. 8 Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. 9 As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house. 10 Moreover he said unto me, Son of man, all my words that I shall speak unto thee receive in thine heart, and hear with thine ears. 11 And go, get thee to them of the captivity, unto the children of thy people, and speak unto them, and tell them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear. 12 Then the spirit took me up, and I heard behind me a voice of a great rushing, saying, Blessed be the glory of the LORD from his place. 13 I heard also the noise of the wings of the living creatures that touched one another, and the noise of the wheels over against them, and a noise of a great rushing. 14 So the spirit lifted me up, and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; but the hand of the LORD was strong upon me.

God did not send him to foreign nations nor to a people of strange dialect, but sent him to his own people, to the nation that has the law of God. But, sadly, it was a disobedient nation that refused to listen to the law that Moses received on Mount Sinai, and continued to reject the word of God on the tongues of the prophets... until the Word Himself came, and they rejected Him.

entries.section: 2. The difficulty of the work:

paragraphs.text: God punishes them in an indirect way, saying to Ezekiel: "Surely, had I sent thee to them, they would have hearkened unto thee" [6]. And indeed, when the Word came, the nations of foreign race received Him.

entries.section: 2. The difficulty of the work:

paragraphs.text: Ezekiel's mission was exceedingly difficult, "for all the house of Israel are impudent and hardhearted" [7]. This is the effect of sin in the life of man: it makes his heart hard as stone and his forehead hard; he does not want to hear the divine voice but resists it violently without shame. But God gives His servants strength, for He says: "Behold, I have made thy face strong against their faces, and thy forehead strong against their foreheads. As an adamant harder than flint have I made thy forehead: fear them not, neither be dismayed at their looks, though they be a rebellious house" [8-9]. Though evil is violent by nature, it cannot stand to the end, for good shatters it, as light scatters darkness and truth falsehood, and the Kingdom of God remains forever while the kingdom of the devil is for a time. Thus, whenever the servant hides in God as his refuge, the enemy of good cannot stand before him.

entries.section: 2. The difficulty of the work:

paragraphs.text: When Ezekiel received the word of God he heard behind him a voice of a great rushing [12]; these are the heavenly powers working in secret within his heart, thundering to shatter the evil that hardened the hearts of sinners. He heard the noise of the wings of the living creatures that touched one another. It is as though the heavenly creation, which works together in one spirit, also supports us by its prayers on our behalf. As for the noise of the wheels, it is the authority of the Gospel word, which captivates hearts and draws them.

entries.section: 2. The difficulty of the work:

paragraphs.text: With all these resources, the divine heavenly resources and the support of the heavenly ones besides the power of the word itself, the service is full of toil and pain... The inner bitterness of heart for the sake of shattered souls is enough, for the prophet says: "So the spirit lifted me up, and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit; but the hand of the LORD was strong upon me" [14]. It is as though he were saying with the psalmist: "Despondency hath taken hold of me because of the sinners who have departed from thy law" (Ps 118).

Ezekiel had to declare the message among those who had suffered the captivity, and they had either to receive the word of God as a savour of life unto life or a savour of death unto death. Sadly, they did not benefit from the captivity, nor were their hearts softened by the chastisement, nor did they listen to the word of God in the midst of their exile, but increased in hardness and stubbornness against God and His prophets. God made clear to him that they would refuse to listen to him, and would even resist and persecute him... It is their responsibility, not his. As for him, he must enjoy a divine power that makes him hard as adamant to face their hardness [8].

The Spirit of the Lord carried him from before the throne to bring him to the captives to serve them [12-15], that he might realize that his movements are not according to his human will but according to God's plan... that he is carried by the Spirit. He came, and his soul was filled with bitterness, and the hand of the Lord was strong upon him [14]. Perhaps the secret of his soul's bitterness sprang from comparing his standing before the divine throne, sharing the praises of the heavenly ones, with his transfer to the captives, whose peace and joy of heart sin had shattered; he became embittered in his soul, saying with the Apostle Peter: "Lord, it is good for us to be here." He did not want to leave the divine throne. Perhaps he was also embittered because he felt the people's deprivation of what he had seen and experienced by standing before the divine throne!

entries.section: 3. His responsibility as a watchman:

paragraphs.text: 15 Then I came to them of the captivity at Telabib, that dwelt by the river of Chebar, and I sat where they sat, and remained there astonished among them seven days. 16 And it came to pass at the end of seven days, that the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 17 Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me. 18 When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 19 Yet if thou warn the wicked, and he turn not from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul. 20 Again, When a righteous man doth turn from his righteousness, and commit iniquity, and I lay a stumblingblock before him, he shall die: because thou hast not given him warning, he shall die in his sin, and his righteousness which he hath done shall not be remembered; but his blood will I require at thine hand. 21 Nevertheless if thou warn the righteous man, that the righteous sin not, and he doth not sin, he shall surely live, because he is warned; also thou hast delivered thy soul.

entries.section: 3. His responsibility as a watchman:

paragraphs.text: When Ezekiel had eaten the word of God and been satisfied with it, he remained among the captives seven days in bewilderment, not knowing what to do, and the voice of the Lord came to him: "Son of man, I have made thee a watchman" [17]. It is as though two things are necessarily required for appointing the watchman: that he eat the word of God, and that he live seven days among his people. The number 7 points to perfection, or the completeness of the days of the week; it is as though the watchman is not an employee who performs a work for wages, who works for a while and rests, but truly a loving man who throws himself among his people all the days of his life, knowing no rest for himself. When the Apostle Paul wanted to describe the first leader of the people, that is, Moses the prophet, he said of him: "By faith Moses, when he was come to years, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter; choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season; esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward" (Heb 11:24-26). Thus Moses threw himself into the disgrace of his people, counting that better than living in the comfort of Pharaoh's palace, leaving every temporary pleasure for the sake of the eternal reward. These are the marks of the spiritual watchman. He works among his people as their servant, bearing their reproach, seeking not his own but what is for their comfort.
His being called "watchman" is a sign of the existence of a spiritual war; in his service he washes the feet of others and fights Satan and his hosts.

In ancient times cities were often built on hills, and a tower was built on the city walls, and in the tower was a watchman who could track the movements of any enemy coming toward the city and warn the people; then the gates of the city were closed and the army prepared for war.

As for God's commandment to him, it is: "Hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me" [17]. As a watchman he must bear a spirit of discernment through his keeping of the word of the Lord and his fellowship with God, so that he does not warn from himself but by what he hears from the mouth of God, and does not speak in his own name but in the name of God ("from me"). By this he can warn with all strength, without fear, flattery or compromise, lest souls perish and their blood be required of him.

God made clear to His servant the extent of his responsibility for the perishing of every soul he fails to warn out of negligence, a matter that has terrified the servants of God throughout the ages. Therefore when St. Ambrose felt that the Emperor Theodosius had committed an error, he hastened to write to him warning him, saying to him: [Can I keep silent?! For my conscience would be bound, my speech taken from me, and I would be in the worst state I could be in...! If the priest does not speak with the one who sins... the sinner dies in his sin, and the priest himself is subject to punishment because he did not warn against the error]. Again he writes to him thus: [I beg you to listen patiently to what I say. If I am unworthy to be heard by you, I am also unworthy to offer sacrifices on your behalf, you who have trusted in your vows and prayers... It is not for the emperor to refuse freedom of speech, nor for the priest not to say what he thinks].

St. John Chrysostom has presented to us a wonderful example of the watchman's care not for the congregation as a whole but for each soul as if it were the whole congregation, saying: [Each one of you, in my eyes, is equal to the whole city].

Again he says: [Let no one say to me that many have fulfilled the commandment, for I do not seek this, but I want everyone to do so. I cannot catch my breath until I see that fulfilled! For if one man committed fornication among the Corinthians, Paul sighed as though the whole city were lost].

St. Paul felt his responsibility as a watchman, and he says to the presbyters of the Church in Ephesus: "Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men. For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God... Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears" (Acts 20:26-27, 31). And as Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles, says: [From whose blood is the Apostle pure...? The blood of souls, of course, and not the blood of bodies]. He also says: [We must fear lest the souls of many perish because of the famine of the word of God resulting from our negligence, and it be required of our souls on the day of judgment].

entries.section: 4. Solitude before the work:

paragraphs.text: 22 And the hand of the LORD was there upon me; and he said unto me, Arise, go forth into the plain, and I will there talk with thee. 23 Then I arose, and went forth into the plain: and, behold, the glory of the LORD stood there, as the glory which I saw by the river of Chebar: and I fell on my face.

As he acts as a watchman, the Lord commanded him not to hasten to begin the work but to go forth into the plain to speak with him [22], and there He showed him His heavenly glory again, as he had seen by the river Chebar. For the success of the mission does not rest on the abundance of work but on the quality of the servant; he is obliged to be sanctified through his solitude with God, to lift his heart to the divine glories and so present to the people in his life "the power of the heavenly life."

Going forth into the plain to behold the glory of the Lord is necessary for every servant; therefore after the Apostle Paul was called to service he committed himself to stay three years in the wilderness in a long solitude with God to prepare for the apostolic work. St. Augustine speaks of the servants' commitment to spiritual solitude without solitude hindering the work or the work hindering the life of solitude, saying: [Those to whom works of good and the care of souls have been entrusted are obliged to bring to people a witness of the other life (contemplation); therefore they must devote themselves to the study and contemplation of the truth and of eternal life. Nor is it fair that the life of contemplation should be a cause for hindering a man from performing the tasks of the Church].

For the success of our service we need the Lord to be manifested in our hearts, and to enjoy the divine presence, not once only but from time to time, so that we enjoy continual new visions that reveal the glory of God, His power and His resources... and we are assured that He is working in us and through us. He is always present within us, manifesting Himself continually in our depths.

entries.section: 5. A time to keep silence and a time to speak:

paragraphs.text: 24 Then the spirit entered into me, and set me upon my feet, and spake with me, and said unto me, Go, shut thyself within thine house. 25 But thou, O son of man, behold, they shall put bands upon thee, and shall bind thee with them, and thou shalt not go out among them: 26 And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house. 27 But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; He that heareth, let him hear; and he that forbeareth, let him forbear: for they are a rebellious house.

The vision was repeated and the prophet Ezekiel's falling on his face was repeated, and the divine Spirit also entered him to raise him up and he heard this message: "Go, shut thyself within thine house... And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house. But when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth, and thou shalt say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD" [24-27]. Thus the Lord wanted him not to work by human zeal but to be silent and not speak until He permits him to speak, so that he speaks at the time the Lord sees fit and with the words of the Lord and in His name. Although as a watchman he is condemned for his silence in the face of evil, he must learn what the wise man said: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak" (Eccl 3:7). As St. Ambrose says: [Weigh your speech and measure your words], and also: [The wise man in his speech takes into consideration what he says, to whom he speaks, and the circumstances of place and time... Thus there must be a measure for keeping silence as for speaking]. Father Gregory the Great says: [The shepherd must be discreet in his silence and profitable in his speech].
Feed me with Your commandment, O desire of my heart!
*Feed me with Your commandment, O desire of my heart!
Stretch out Your hand and give me Your commandment as heavenly bread.
I am a child, even an infant; I will not accept food from anyone but You!
You are more tender to me than my parents, O Savior of my soul!

*Your commandment is hard, O Savior of my soul, Your cross is heavy, and Your way is a narrow affliction, but from Your hands Your commandment becomes bread and honey of the bees, Your cross becomes glory, and Your way a new heaven!
*You sent Your prophet carrying Your word to Your stubborn people; grant me to carry Your commandment to every soul, however stubborn!
With the receiving of Your word a great rushing took place in heaven.
Let heaven thunder and shake every hardness in my heart and in their hearts.
Let the shaken earthly nature be removed from them, and let them enjoy an eternal heavenly life.
*Your prophet presented Your word to a stubborn people, and his soul became embittered.
Was he perhaps bitter in soul because he did not want to leave the beholding of Your chariot?!
Was he perhaps bitter in soul because he came into contact with the stubbornness of humanity?!
Grant me, in the midst of my soul's bitterness, to see Your heavens; grant me, in the midst of my sorrow, to touch the repentance of many.
My heart rejoices in Your divine work in them and through them, O divine Word.
Your prophet remained among the captives seven days; grant me to spend all the days of my exile working in Your vineyard.
I am not a hired servant counting the time, but a son who longs to work in my Father's vineyard.
*Teach me, O divine Word:
When shall I be alone with You to know Your mysteries?!
And when shall I work in the vineyard to serve Your people?!
Grant me in my solitude not to forget Your people, and in my service not to cease contemplating Your mysteries.
*Guide me, O true Word, for I do not know when to be silent and when to speak, how to be silent and how to speak?!
Here I am in Your hands; be my leader who works in me.

entries.section: 1. The shaving of the prophet’s hair:

paragraphs.text: 1 “And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber’s razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair. 2 Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind; and I will draw out a sword after them. 3 Thou shalt also take thereof a few in number, and bind them in thy skirts. 4 Then take of them again, and cast them into the midst of the fire, and burn them in the fire; for thereof shall a fire come forth into all the house of Israel.”
“And thou, son of man, take thee a sharp knife, take thee a barber’s razor, and cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard: then take thee balances to weigh, and divide the hair.

Thou shalt burn with fire a third part in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are fulfilled: and thou shalt take a third part, and smite about it with a knife: and a third part thou shalt scatter in the wind” [1-2].

God commanded Moses to speak thus to the priests, the sons of Aaron: “They shall not make baldness upon their head, neither shall they shave off the corner of their beard, nor make any cuttings in their flesh. They shall be holy unto their God, and not profane the name of their God: for the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and the bread of their God, they do offer: therefore they shall be holy” (Lev 21:5-6). The divine commandment was clear and explicit that no razor should touch the head or beard of a priest, for he is holy to the Lord. For the hair left on a woman’s head is her adornment, but for a man it is a sign that he is not occupied with temporal matters, having consecrated every breath of his life to the priestly service. Therefore the command given to the prophet Ezekiel is a declaration of the defilement of the priests at that time, and of the Lord’s rejection of their sacrifices, their offerings and their prayers.

When the Lord wished in former times to save the people, the angel of the Lord appeared to the wife of Manoah, who was barren, and said to her: “For, lo, thou shalt conceive, and bear a son; and no razor shall come on his head: for the child shall be a Nazarite unto God from the womb: and he shall begin to deliver Israel out of the hand of the Philistines” (Judg 13:5). When this man’s hair was shaved off, the strength of the Lord departed from him and he became weak (Judg 16:17); indeed the Lord Himself departed from him (Judg 16:20), and he lost his eyes and was bound with fetters of brass, and became like an ox grinding in the prison house (Judg 16:21), and he was a mockery and a laughingstock to the pagans! But now it is God Himself who commands the shaving of the head and the beard, as a sign of His departure from the priests of His people, of their loss of spiritual sight, of their entering into captivity and of their becoming a laughingstock of the nations and the object of their derision.

The complete shaving of the hair signifies God’s refusal to enter into any relationship with them through the priests or the prophets; He accepts no offering and hears no prayer until He has disciplined them for their wickedness. It also signifies His rejection of His people because of their insistence on sin. If the Lord is the Head, then our life consists in abiding in Him. So the removal of the hair is the end of the people’s abiding in the source of their life. In this St. Jerome says: [The prophet Isaiah speaks of a sharp razor that shaves the head of sinners and the hair of their feet (Isa 7:20); he shaves his head as a type of Jerusalem, which had become a harlot (Ezek 5:1-5), a sign that everything in her had become insensible and life had been taken away from her.]

The complete shaving of the hair signifies intense grief, especially in the case of a death, and this was defilement in the eyes of the Lord. Therefore He warned His people, saying: “Ye are the children of the LORD your God: ye shall not cut yourselves, nor make any baldness between your eyes for the dead. For thou art holy unto the LORD thy God, and the LORD hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself” (Deut 14:1-2). But now Jerusalem had become as one reckoned among the dead. And since His people rejected Him, He commanded them, in the person of Ezekiel, to defile themselves by shaving the hair of their heads.

The shaving of the hair is also a sign of shame, humiliation and slavery. A man becomes without dignity, with no authority even over his own hair, whether to leave it or to shave it. For this reason the heads of slaves were shaved completely, and also those of kings when they were taken captive. This is what sin does to a man: it strips him of all authority and brings him down from the state of king and power to the shame of slavery, falling into captivity and humiliation. The servants of David were ashamed to meet their king because Hanun, king of the children of Ammon, suspected them and shaved off their beards, so they stayed at Jericho until their beards were grown, and then returned... Likewise a man cannot meet the Lord, his heavenly King, while he is in the shame and disgrace of sin; rather he waits until he declares his repentance, receives forgiveness and recovers his dignity, and so becomes able to meet God and all His heavenly and earthly hosts.

The shaving of the hair with a sharp knife signifies a bloody war, in which God allowed the hard-hearted Chaldeans to invade Judah, according to what His divine providence required. He allowed this because Judah had rebelled against God: a third would perish in the siege of Jerusalem, a third would be killed mercilessly by the sword at the hands of the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar, and the remaining third would be scattered over the face of the earth among the peoples.

As for the weighing of the hair, it is a sign that what befalls the people of hunger, thirst, falling by the sword and scattering among the peoples does not take place randomly or by mere chance, but by divine ordering, and the Lord’s balances are just, faithful and exact.

“The LORD weigheth the hearts” (Prov 21:2) and the spirits (Prov 16:2); He before whose eyes are the ways of man, and “he pondereth all his goings” (Prov 5:21); who weighs the winds and weighs the waters by measure (Job 28:25), and comprehends the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighs the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance (Isa 40:12). His balances are true and just; He cannot bear deceit or partiality. This is the nature of God, which He desires to pour out into the lives of His children; therefore He often repeats the commandments: “Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thine house divers measures, a great and a small. But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have” (Deut 25:13-15); “Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good” (Prov 20:23); “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Prov 11:1). God weighs our lives and, sadly, finds them “in the balances they go up” (Ps 62:9), or as the wise Daniel said to King Belshazzar: “Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting” (Dan 5:6). And now, what does the Lord do toward us, who have been found so? He bears the secret of our lack; He bears our iniquity upon Himself and comes forward to the balance, and behold, He is priced as a slave, He who is the Judge who judges the whole world. In bitterness He says: “So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver” (Zech 11:12). The Lord is valued as a slave, while the slave stands in his self-righteousness to say: “Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity” (Job 31:6). The Perfect One was weighed, bearing our lack, and came under shame, while man in the pride of his heart wishes to be justified in the balances before God.

In any case, Ezekiel’s hair was weighed as a symbol of the people fallen under the weight of sin, and found deserving of hunger, thirst, the sword and scattering... These are the fruits of uncleanness and evil.

Although the people were found wanting in the balance, God does not forget the very few among them, those who, because of their faithfulness to Him and their obedience to His words, He keeps in the skirt of His garment, under His care. This remnant perhaps refers to the remnant that was left in Jerusalem under the leadership of Gedaliah. And perhaps it refers to the remnant that remains faithful to the Lord in the days of the false prophet or the Antichrist. They are the hidden company of the Lord, kept and concealed in Him; He knows them by name and puts a hedge around them so that none of them is lost, and the wicked enemy does not snatch them away. But sadly, the Lord commanded that a few of this small number be burned, because after entering under His care they rejected Him. Of these the Apostle said that they began in the Spirit but are being made perfect by the flesh (Gal 3:3). Therefore the Lord instructs us to endure to the end (Mt 10:12), and warns us of the last days, when it is feared that even the elect may be deceived (Mt 24:24).

entries.section: 2. The secret of her punishment:

paragraphs.text: 5 “Thus saith the Lord GOD; This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations and countries that are round about her. 6 And she hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations, and my statutes more than the countries that are round about her: for they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them. 7 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Because ye multiplied more than the nations that are round about you, and have not walked in my statutes, neither have kept my judgments, neither have done according to the judgments of the nations that are round about you,” God, like a father disciplining his children, reveals to them the secret of their punishment. He is not a tyrannical master nor an avenger; rather, even in the severity of His discipline He desires our return and repentance... Therefore He shows us our weaknesses so that we may abandon them.

entries.section: 2. The secret of her punishment:

paragraphs.text: Two things grieve the heart of God: the broken commandment and the defiled temple. Concerning the commandment He says: “For they have refused my judgments and my statutes, they have not walked in them” [6]. And it is strange that when the believer falls into disobedience he becomes more wicked than the unbeliever, for the Lord says: “She hath changed my judgments into wickedness more than the nations” [6]. As for the defiling of the temple, He says: “Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity” [11].

The keeping of the commandment and worship (the temple) are two things that go together and are joined in the life of the believer. By obeying the commandment we gain boldness to stand before God, and standing before Him in worship supports our life in obedience to the commandment. Whoever thinks that he keeps the commandment apart from the spirit of worship deceives himself, and so does whoever thinks that he pleases the Lord by worship without walking in obedience to the commandment.

entries.section: 3. A public punishment:

paragraphs.text: 8 “Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I, even I, am against thee, and will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations.” When He sent to the people of Judah the prophet Jeremiah to rebuke them for their sins, He said to him: “Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem” (Jer 2:1), as though He wished to whisper in their ears so that they might repent without anyone knowing what they had done; but when they did not listen, He asked him to stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and proclaim the word of rebuke (Jer 7:1), and when they still did not listen, He was compelled to make His chastisements of His people public before all the nations. They sinned openly without shame, and He tried to correct them without wounding their feelings, but in the face of their growing arrogance He says: “I will execute judgments in the midst of thee in the sight of the nations” [8], “Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by. So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that are round about thee” [14-15].

Jerusalem became a lesson to the nations around her, and a visible lesson to the whole world. For the holy God does not accept sin, nor does He make peace with it, even if His people commit it in the holy city!

God, as the Lover of mankind, covers our sins and weaknesses once and many times, but when He finds our healing in exposing us, He announces His severe chastisements upon us. This is also what the Church does with her children and servants: she heals with love and covers, but if the matter calls for public discipline she does not refrain, for the sake of the salvation of her children. In the apostolic age the Apostle judged publicly the one who fell into sin with his father’s wife, saying: “It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father’s wife... For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed, In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus... Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened” (1 Cor 5:1-7).

entries.section: 4. A unique punishment:

paragraphs.text: 9 “And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations. 10 Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds. 11 Wherefore, as I live, saith the Lord GOD; Surely, because thou hast defiled my sanctuary with all thy detestable things, and with all thine abominations, therefore will I also diminish thee; neither shall mine eye spare, neither will I have any pity. 12 A third part of thee shall die with the pestilence, and with famine shall they be consumed in the midst of thee: and a third part shall fall by the sword round about thee; and I will scatter a third part into all the winds, and I will draw out a sword after them.”

They vied with one another in evil and surpassed the nations; therefore God also disciplines them with unique chastisements: “And I will do in thee that which I have not done, and whereunto I will not do any more the like, because of all thine abominations. Therefore the fathers shall eat the sons in the midst of thee, and the sons shall eat their fathers; and I will execute judgments in thee, and the whole remnant of thee will I scatter into all the winds” [9-10].

This is the bitterest punishment under which believers can fall: that one of them eats the other, indeed that the father eats his son and the son his father! For when the grace of God abandons them, corruption creeps into them from within, and through divisions and schisms one member eats another, even if he is bound to him by ties of flesh or of spirit, and finally nothing is left of them except ashes that the Lord scatters into every wind!

I say that the fruit of sin is that the community eats one another instead of supporting one another; indeed division creeps into the man himself, so that he rises up against himself, loses his peace, his balance and his vitality, and the man, because of sin, becomes like ashes of no value, scattered by the winds in every direction!

entries.section: 5. A divine punishment:

paragraphs.text: 13 “Thus shall mine anger be accomplished, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the LORD have spoken it in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury in them. 14 Moreover I will make thee waste, and a reproach among the nations that are round about thee, in the sight of all that pass by. 15 So it shall be a reproach and a taunt, an instruction and an astonishment unto the nations that are round about thee, when I shall execute judgments in thee in anger and in fury and in furious rebukes. I the LORD have spoken it.”

entries.section: 5. A divine punishment:

paragraphs.text: The Lord assured Judah that this unique public chastisement does not come from the prophet, who is not speaking against them, but from God Himself: “I the LORD have spoken it” [15].

Although the Chaldeans fight against you and take your people captive, in truth they are an instrument in the hand of God, who raises the nations against His people to discipline them. Therefore He affirms: “Behold, I, even I, am against thee” [9], repeating the phrase “I the LORD have spoken it” and the like about 14 times in this book.

For this reason, when Absalom rose up against his father David and the latter fled, Shimei the son of Gera came out against him, cursing and casting stones at David, and all the servants of the king, and the people and the mighty men around him; then Abishai said to the king: “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head” (2 Sam 16:9). But David, in wisdom and humility, said: “Let him curse, because the LORD hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?... It may be that the LORD will look on mine affliction, and that the LORD will requite me good for his cursing this day.” St. John Chrysostom sees in the plots of others against us an opportunity for repentance, for he says: [If we sin, God raises our enemies against us to discipline us. Therefore it is fitting for us not to fight them, but to examine ourselves and instruct ourselves. Let us accept sufferings as we accept medicines from the physician for our salvation, and as we accept discipline from a father, so that we may be glorified.]

entries.section: 6. A punishment in stages:

paragraphs.text: 16 “When I shall send upon them the evil arrows of famine, which shall be for their destruction, and which I will send to destroy you: and I will increase the famine upon you, and will break your staff of bread: 17 So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee; and pestilence and blood shall pass through thee; and I will bring the sword upon thee. I the LORD have spoken it.”

In His longsuffering and love, God began with secret speaking to His people, then with open speaking, and finally was compelled to open chastisement; and here too He disciplines in stages, that perhaps they may repent and He may remove the pain from them. He allows them to hunger, then increases His pressure upon them until they are in need of bread. And when they do not return, He stirs up the wild beasts against them to devour their children, then He allows pestilence and the shedding of blood... He seeks not vengeance but repentance, by every way.
Establish me in You, O tender Disciplinarian!
* Establish me in You, O tender Disciplinarian!

You allowed Your prophet Ezekiel to shave off all the hair of his head, to declare Your intense grief over the corruption of Your people as though they were dead, and to threaten Your people that You would remove them from You as hair from the head, and to reject their priesthood, which had become defiled, and to assure them that they live as captive slaves with shaven heads!
* Discipline me... but do not hand me over to another than You!
For You are the tender Disciplinarian!
* You disciplined me in secret and I was not restrained; behold, You expose me among my people, indeed even among the nations...
Let it be... but do not deprive me of Your salvation!
For You are the tender Disciplinarian!

entries.section: 1. A prophecy against the mountains of Israel:

paragraphs.text: 1 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 “Son of man, set thy face toward the mountains of Israel, and prophesy unto them, 3 And say, Ye mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD; Thus saith the Lord GOD to the mountains, and to the hills, to the valleys, and to the lowlands; Behold, I, even I, will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your high places. 4 And your altars shall be desolate, and your sun images shall be broken: and I will cast down your slain men before your idols. 5 And I will lay the dead carcases of the children of Israel before their idols; and I will scatter your bones round about your altars. 6 In all your dwellingplaces the cities shall be laid waste, and the high places shall be desolate; that your altars may be laid waste and made desolate, and your idols may be broken and cease, and your sun images may be cut down, and your works may be abolished. 7 And the slain shall fall in the midst of you, and ye shall know that I am the LORD.

The Jews took from the pagans their worship of idols on the mountains, hills, rivers and valleys. Therefore the Lord asked the prophet Ezekiel to direct his gaze toward the mountains of Israel, which had been defiled by pagan worship, and to prophesy against them. He looks like a judge who looks toward the accused in order to pass sentence on him face to face, to shake his foundations and destroy them.

Mountains have a symbolic meaning in the Holy Bible. For “the earth” often signifies in the Holy Bible the soul that has descended to earthly thought, so that the earthly body with its lusts has taken it captive and bound it to material things, whereas “the mountains” often signify in the Holy Bible souls lifted above earthly things to dwell with Him in the heavenly places, a holy, heavenly Church. For this reason God often ascribes the mountain to Himself and calls it “his holy mountain” (Ps 2:6), (Ps 99:9; Isa 65:11, 25; Joel 2:1; Obad 16), and the Holy Bible also calls it “Jerusalem, thy holy mountain” (Dan 9:16; Isa 66:20), “Zion my holy mountain” (Joel 3:17).

The two angels asked Lot to flee to the mountain lest he perish (Gen 9:17), as though asking him to rise above temporal things lest they ensnare him in their whirlpool. And the psalmist longed to dwell in the holy hill of the Lord (Ps 15:1), that is, for his heart to be lifted up on high, where it meets God who dwells in the heights and who answers him (Ps 30:4).

The soul that becomes a holy mountain becomes like Mount Horeb, where the Lord comes to it, not to give it His Law engraved on stones as to Moses, but to engrave His commandment on its heart by the Holy Spirit. The Lord sits in it as He sat on the mount to teach the multitudes with His words, drawing them to Himself with authority (Mt 5). It becomes like the mount of temptation, on which the Lord Himself ascends to lead the spiritual battle against Satan, shattering his authority, so that the soul gains the ability to overcome and the angels come to minister to it. It becomes like Mount Tabor, where the soul enjoys fellowship with the men of the Old Testament (Moses and Elijah) and the men of the New Testament (Peter, James and John) in the presence of the Lord Christ Himself, who overshadows it with His bright cloud and reveals His radiance to it within. It becomes like the Mount of Olives, where the Lord sits in it weeping over His fallen children who killed the prophets and stoned His messengers, so that it becomes a center of work and spiritual service; or rather it becomes like Mount Golgotha, enjoying the Cross of the Lord Christ planted within it, sharing with its Bridegroom His sufferings and crucifixion so as to enjoy the power of His resurrection. In short, the mountains mentioned in the Holy Bible hold memories that move the soul to enjoy, in one form or another, the life of union with God in Christ Jesus.

St. Jerome sees that these holy mountains are the prophets and the apostles, for he says: [We interpret the mountains in two ways: in the Old Testament they are the prophets, and in the New Testament the apostles. Of these mountains the Holy Bible says: “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” (Ps 120:1). On these mountains the city of God is established, for “a city that is set on an hill cannot be hid” (Mt 5:12). And we also, who were in darkness and the shadow of death, have been shone upon by the Lord from His eternal mountains, that is, through His prophets and apostles.]

And just as the Lord God raises His children as holy mountains in which He dwells, so the enemy of good raises from his servants defiled and stumbling mountains. If the holy mountain means the soul’s rising to the heavenly places by the Holy Spirit, then the evil mountain means the pride of the soul and its disobedience to the divine commandment. So instead of the soul being a mountain to which the Lord goes to pray (Mk 6:46), “the hill which God desireth to dwell in for ever” (Ps 68:16), it becomes defiled, a place where swine feed (Lk 8:32). And instead of the soul being that mountain to which the Church goes up with her Bridegroom as on Mount Tabor, it becomes a cause of wandering (Heb 11:38). Therefore the Lord declares His wrath against the evil mountains and shakes their foundations, or as the psalmist says: “the mountains are carried into the midst of the seas” (Ps 46:2), “What ails you, O mountains, that you skipped like rams?” (Ps 114:2). The Lord threatens these mountains, saying: “Behold, I am against thee, O destroying mountain, saith the LORD, which destroyest all the earth: and I will stretch out mine hand upon thee, and roll thee down from the rocks, and will make thee a burnt mountain. And they shall not take of thee a stone for a corner, nor a stone for foundations; but thou shalt be desolate for ever, saith the LORD” (Jer 51:25-26); as He also says: “I hated Esau, and laid his mountains and his heritage waste for the wolves of the wilderness” (Mal 1:3), “Lift ye up a banner upon the bare mountain, exalt the voice unto them” (Isa 13:2).

The people turned aside to pagan worship, so the Lord threatened them through the prophet with evil coming upon every place used for evil, whether mountain or hill, valley or river. The sword extends to the doers of evil, so that they are killed and their works are blotted out, their cities become waste and desolate, their high places are destroyed, their altars laid waste and their sun images broken (perhaps the canopies used for protection from the sun during worship, though the English translations say “the images that are worshiped”), and their bones are scattered around their altars as a sign of their defilement (2 Kgs 23:16). Thus the worshipers, the object of their worship and the place of worship itself are all shattered.

This is the prophecy that was directed against the mountains of Israel, and it is a bitter threat in order to move them to repentance. It is a prophecy standing in every generation against the arrogant soul: God destroys its high places, that is, He shatters the pride and haughtiness of its heart; He lays waste its altars, that is, He shatters its emotions which it has misused; He breaks its sun images, that is, He exposes it in the middle of the day and no longer covers for it (or perhaps by the sun images he meant the idols belonging to the worship of the sun). He casts down its slain before its idols, that is, He humbles it before those with whom it commits sin; its bones are scattered around its altar, that is, He declares its death spiritually, psychologically and bodily and the defilement of its life, so that all loathe it; He makes its dwelling a desolation, that is, He leaves its heart desolate, without satisfaction; and He blots out its works, a sign of the removal of all vitality and energy for work within it. This discipline is in fact the natural fruit of sin in the life of man: it kills him, kills his inner energies and shatters every possibility in him!

Here we notice that the Promised Land, flowing with milk and honey, which bore witness to God’s good pleasure in His believers, turns into a mass grave. Instead of bearing fruit, it becomes a place of death.

On another side, God threatens to kill them beside the altar of the demons, to prove to them its inability to help... Perhaps He wished to show them His justice: since they defiled His temple with idols, He allows the idols to be defiled by killing them in the pagan temples and turning these into graves that carry corruption.

entries.section: 2. His acceptance of the repentant remnant:

paragraphs.text: 8 “Yet will I leave a remnant, that ye may have some that shall escape the sword among the nations, when ye shall be scattered through the countries. 9 And they that escape of you shall remember me among the nations whither they shall be carried captives, when I have broken their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations. 10 And they shall know that I am the LORD, and that I have not said in vain that I would do this evil unto them.

entries.section: 2. His acceptance of the repentant remnant:

paragraphs.text: Each time He threatens the community or the whole people, He does not forget to stress His care for the repentant remnant who return to Him, despite their small number, those who are saved from the punishment not by accepting the discipline (the captivity) but by their repentance from their sins: “When I have broken their whorish heart, which hath departed from me, and their eyes, which go a whoring after their idols: and they shall lothe themselves for the evils which they have committed in all their abominations” [9]. They sinned like their brothers and fell into fornication, idolatry and every abomination, but they accepted the Lord’s discipline with wisdom, so that their hearts were broken by repentance and they regretted, unable to bear themselves because of what they had done. Therefore the Lord returns to them to save them, “and they shall know that I am the LORD” [10]... that is, He grants them His divine knowledge.

Truly, there is no way to our salvation except repentance, which blots out all our faults by the merits of the precious Blood through the Holy Spirit. Therefore St. Mark the Ascetic says: [God does not judge us because we have sinned, but He judges us because we have not repented.]

entries.section: 3. The effects of evil:

paragraphs.text: 11 “Thus saith the Lord GOD; Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas for all the evil abominations of the house of Israel! for they shall fall by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence. 12 He that is far off shall die of the pestilence; and he that is near shall fall by the sword; and he that remaineth and is besieged shall die by the famine: thus will I accomplish my fury upon them. 13 Then shall ye know that I am the LORD, when their slain men shall be among their idols round about their altars, upon every high hill, in all the tops of the mountains, and under every green tree, and under every thick oak, the place where they did offer sweet savour to all their idols. 14 So will I stretch out my hand upon them, and make the land desolate and waste, from the wilderness to Diblah, in all their habitations: and they shall know that I am the LORD.”

entries.section: 3. The effects of evil:

paragraphs.text: The Lord commanded him to clap his hand and stamp the ground with his feet like a stubborn child who has no strength or power, groaning over all their abominations, especially since the fruit of evil had begun to come upon them, killing by the sword, hunger and pestilence. It is as though the divine wrath had come upon them, so that people rose up against them, and the earth declared its anger, and all nature with it. The discipline will be more severe in the places used for pagan worship: the high hills, the tops of the mountains and under the shade of the trees, especially the oak... where they used to offer “sweet savour to all their idols” [13], which became for them the savour of death!

He declared that devastation creeps over the land from the wilderness to Diblah. Some see it as a town in the place of modern Dibl, north of Galilee, but the prevailing opinion is that it is Riblah, a city in the land of Hamath (2 Kgs 23:33; 25:20-21), as though by saying “from the wilderness to Diblah” he meant from the farthest south to the farthest north. Perhaps he also wished to declare the bitterness of what would happen to them in the person of their king: when Zedekiah was arrested after fleeing from Jerusalem, he was brought to Nebuchadnezzar, who was at Riblah, and he put out his eyes and bound him in chains to send him to Babylon (2 Kgs 25:6 etc.; Jer 39:5-7; 25:9-11).
The holy mountain!
* Wonderful are Your works, O Lord!
You have made me a mountain holy to You, I who am dust and sand!

Count me as Mount Horeb on which You declare Your Law, and as Mount Tabor on which You are transfigured in Your radiance, and as Mount Golgotha on which You offer the surpassing sacrifice of Your love!
* On the mountains Israel set up his idols like the nations, and defiled the high places with his abominations!
In Your love You discipline, bringing a sword and destroying the high places, and the cities turn into desolation!
But You do not forget the holy remnant, for You are the merciful God!
Remove from my mountains all abominations; burn with the fire of Your Holy Spirit all the thorns of sin!
Sanctify me, and count me Your holy mountain!

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: 1 Moreover the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 “Also, thou son of man, thus saith the Lord GOD unto the land of Israel; An end, the end is come upon the four corners of the land. 3 Now is the end come upon thee, and I will send mine anger upon thee, and will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense upon thee all thine abominations. 4 And mine eye shall not spare thee, neither will I have pity: but I will recompense thy ways upon thee, and thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee: and ye shall know that I am the LORD. 5 Thus saith the Lord GOD; An evil, an only evil, behold, is come. 6 An end is come, the end is come: it watcheth for thee; behold, it is come. 7 The turn is come unto thee, O thou that dwellest in the land: the time is come, the day of trouble is near, and not the sounding again of the mountains. 8 Now will I shortly pour out my fury upon thee, and accomplish mine anger upon thee: and I will judge thee according to thy ways, and will recompense thee for all thine abominations. 9 And mine eye shall not spare, neither will I have pity: I will recompense thee according to thy ways and thine abominations that are in the midst of thee; and ye shall know that I am the LORD that smiteth. 10 Behold the day, behold, it is come: the circle hath turned about; the rod hath blossomed, pride hath budded. 11 Violence is risen up into a rod of wickedness: none of them shall remain, nor of their multitude, nor of their wealth: neither shall there be wailing for them.

St. Peter the Apostle recorded for us the thinking of the scoffers who walk after their own lusts, those who say: “Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (2 Pet 3:4). And the Apostle Paul rebukes them: “Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Rom 2:4-5).
