Here the Lord affirms that the time of punishment has drawn near, which the Jewish people thought would never happen. Therefore the phrases are repeated in this chapter: “An end, the end is come, now is the end come upon thee (against thee), an evil is come, the time is come, the day is come” [2, 5, 6, 12]. And he spoke of the end from three sides:
a. The end is extremely painful [1-6].

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: b. The end is at the doors [7-10].
c. The end is inevitable, with no escape [10-15].

The end came when their consciences became utterly hardened and there was no longer in their lives the least sign of repentance. Therefore God judges them according to their evil ways and abominations, because they did not listen to His prophets, nor did they repent of their idolatry.

The end is extremely painful, not because God wants the bitterness of their souls, for He still loves them, but because this is the nature of sin itself, its nature being turmoil and distress, for He says: “the day of trouble is near, and not the sounding again of the mountains” [7]. The songs of praise ended, joy was taken from them, and anxiety and distress came with the coming of sin into their lives. This is what He affirms by saying: “I will recompense thy ways upon thee, and thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee” [4]. It is as though the Lord affirms that what befalls her is the very nature of the corruption of sin and the abominations which man has chosen for himself, for it carries its punishment within itself.

This is what St. Augustine affirms as he comments on the words of the psalmist: [“As wax melteth, so let the wicked perish”] (Ps 68:2): [They perish by a kind of fire of their lusts. Here (in the world) there is a kind of hidden punishment of sinners of which the psalm speaks... For evil lust is like burning and fire. Does fire burn a garment while the lust of fornication does not burn the soul?! For the Scripture says of deliberate fornication: “Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?” (Prov 6:27)... And the Apostle says: “Wherefore God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts” (Rom 1:24). See the fire that makes him melt like wax!]

“The turn is come unto thee, O thou that dwellest in the land” [7]. Since the heart of the wicked dwells on the earth and becomes dust, his turn comes with the turning of the wheel of divine judgment, and there is none who can turn it from its course... The day of wrath comes. But whoever lifts his heart by repentance to heaven does not fall under wrath but enjoys the divine mercy.

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: When the wicked who persist in their evil fall under wrath, they do not see the Lord the Shepherd but “the LORD that smiteth,” for He says: “and ye shall know that I am the LORD that smiteth” [9].
When the Lord declares the nearness of the painful end, which is the natural fruit of uncleannesses, He makes clear what the uncleannesses are so that believers may turn back from them.

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: a. Pride: “the rod hath blossomed, pride hath budded” [10]. For the people’s fall into pagan worship or fornication was caused by pride. This is the beginning of the pains of the soul, which shattered the devil and brought him down from the highest heavenly ranks to the abyss, and which drove Adam and Eve out of Paradise. Therefore God humbles the proud, not because He desires to humble them, but in order to cut off from them what belongs to Satan, so that they may, in the spirit of humility, repent, submitting to the divine commandment.

entries.section: 1. The end is at the doors:

paragraphs.text: b. Violence: “Violence is risen up into a rod of wickedness” [11]. If pride touches chiefly man’s relationship with God, violence touches man’s relationship with his brother, and though the two are linked together, both are indicators of hardness of heart as an evil nature that corrupts man’s inner life and consequently his dealings with God and man.

Pride drives man to humiliation with none to be gentle with him, and violence drives him to the loss of what he has with none to have mercy on him: “none of them shall remain, nor of their multitude, nor of their wealth: neither shall there be wailing for them” [11].

entries.section: 2. The end of social life:

paragraphs.text: 12 “The time is come, the day draweth near: let not the buyer rejoice, nor the seller mourn: for wrath is upon all the multitude thereof. 13 For the seller shall not return to that which is sold, although they were yet alive: for the vision is touching the whole multitude thereof, which shall not return; neither shall any strengthen himself in the iniquity of his life. 14 They have blown the trumpet, even to make all ready; but none goeth to the battle: for my wrath is upon all the multitude thereof. 15 The sword is without, and the pestilence and the famine within: he that is in the field shall die with the sword; and he that is in the city, famine and pestilence shall devour him. 16 But they that escape of them shall escape, and shall be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them mourning, every one for his iniquity. 17 All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water. 18 They shall also gird themselves with sackcloth, and horror shall cover them; and shame shall be upon all faces, and baldness upon all their heads. 19 They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be an unclean thing: their silver and their gold shall not be able to deliver them in the day of the wrath of the LORD: they shall not satisfy their souls, neither fill their bowels: because it is the stumblingblock of their iniquity.

entries.section: 2. The end of social life:

paragraphs.text: If our temporal life distracts us from spiritual preparation to meet the Lord, God sometimes allows us distress in all aspects of our temporal life, perhaps so that we may return and think about God’s threats and chastisements. Therefore He speaks to them here of a state of ruin and complete destruction of the city socially and economically: the buyer does not rejoice because he has nothing to buy with, nor the seller because he will not return to his trade; the trumpets are blown for war, but there is no man who rises to fight... a state of total loss! The sword pursues them from without, and pestilence and famine from within, and those who flee are not like strong lions but in the weakness of the doves that fly with constant moaning; they mourn as they see the city utterly ruined. They lose all bodily, psychological and spiritual energy: “All hands shall be feeble, and all knees shall be weak as water.” They enter a state of intense grief like one mourning a dead man, for “they shall also gird themselves with sackcloth... and baldness upon all their heads” [18].

Horror takes hold of them, and their silver and their gold which they had stored up cannot deliver them in the day of the divine wrath. They have lost all their hope, all their strength and all their holiness!

entries.section: 2. The end of social life:

paragraphs.text: Their wealth, which distracted them from attention to the divine commandments and heavenly threats, cannot save them but becomes the cause of their destruction, since they use it in the worship of idols: “They shall cast their silver in the streets, and their gold shall be an unclean thing” [19]. What is silver but the word of God, purified seven times? Instead of keeping it in their hearts and preserving it in their inner storehouses, they cast it into the streets and neglect it. As for gold, which signifies the heavenly things, instead of lifting their lives to fellowship with God so as to experience the heavenly life within them, they stumble over heavenly things and grow in uncleanness!

entries.section: 3. The end of formal religious life:

paragraphs.text: 20 “As for the beauty of his ornament, he set it in majesty: but they made the images of their abominations and of their detestable things therein: therefore have I made it unto them an unclean thing. 21 And I will give it into the hands of the strangers for a prey, and to the wicked of the earth for a spoil; and they shall pollute it. 22 My face will I turn also from them, and they shall pollute my secret place: for the robbers shall enter into it, and defile it. 23 Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence. 24 Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled. 25 Destruction cometh; and they shall seek peace, and there shall be none. 26 Mischief shall come upon mischief, and rumour shall be upon rumour; then shall they seek a vision of the prophet; but the law shall perish from the priest, and counsel from the ancients.

If the former left God because of love of the world, and therefore God allowed the ruin of the city and all that is in it, others were occupied away from God through the formalities of worship, and therefore God allowed the ruin of the visible temple, perhaps that they might care for the inner temple in the heart.
God delivered their cities and their land to be plundered by foreign hands, and behold, He delivers His temple also to strangers.

entries.section: 3. The end of formal religious life:

paragraphs.text: His people defiled His altar with the worship of idols, so the Lord delivered His temple to the foreign soldiers who besieged it, to plunder it, and to the wicked of the earth to spoil it. He turned His face from His house since His children had turned it into a den of robbers, leaving the wicked to do what is not fitting: “My face will I turn also from them, and they shall pollute my secret place: for the robbers shall enter into it, and defile it” [22].

entries.section: 3. The end of formal religious life:

paragraphs.text: The defilement of the altar does not stop at their accepting pagan worship, but extends to their breaking the divine commandment and walking in injustice. Therefore God counts their worship a defilement of His temple, since it comes from a heart stained with blood and full of injustice. They defiled His temple, so He lets strangers defile their holy places, perhaps meaning the temple itself or their houses as sanctuaries. He says: “Make a chain: for the land is full of bloody crimes, and the city is full of violence. Wherefore I will bring the worst of the heathen, and they shall possess their houses: I will also make the pomp of the strong to cease; and their holy places shall be defiled” [23-24]. He allows the preparing of the chain, that is, the fetters for their captivity, for they had bound themselves with the chains of their sins; therefore they are delivered into the hands of the enemies, bound with visible chains of metal. Perhaps He also prepared the chain of His divine justice to punish them!

Besides their worship of idols and their breaking of the commandment, they resort to deceiving themselves with false prophecies. Instead of repentance they ask the prophets and priests for a false and deceptive peace. Therefore false prophets appeared who prophesy not according to God’s command but according to what pleases the desires of the people, and the law perished from the priest and counsel from the ancients... These say “Peace, peace; when there is no peace” (Jer 8:11).

Let every believer beware, and every family, and also every church, for if something forbidden enters, ruin comes and all fall under the wrath of God! And it is said, “There is an accursed thing in the midst of thee, O Israel” (Josh 7:13).

entries.section: 4. The end of the temporal kingship:

paragraphs.text: 27 “The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled: I will do unto them after their way, and according to their deserts will I judge them; and they shall know that I am the LORD.”

“The king shall mourn, and the prince shall be clothed with desolation, and the hands of the people of the land shall be troubled” [27]. Thus man sometimes relies on temporal authority, thinking that the Lord’s chastisements will not touch him; therefore the Lord breaks this temporal authority, and the king mourns... Here he refers to Jehoiachin (Ezek 27:12) and the former kings (Ezek 43:7, 9), as well as to the kings who will rule in the future (Ezek 37:22, 24), but he does not mean King Zedekiah (Ezek 12:12; 21:25). As for the prince (Prince), he means the head of the new community, or the ruling class at that time. As for the people of the land, before the captivity this referred to non-Hebrews (Ezra 4:4; Neh 10:31), but here he means the Jewish people.
How long will you wait, O my soul?!
* Your voice, O my God, has never ceased!
It warns me: the end is at the doors!
You are the Architect of the whole world; You know its secrets; You assure me: heaven and earth shall pass away, and I in my folly grow slack and am humiliated!
* How long will you wait, O my soul?!
Will you flee to the mountains?! Behold, they are shaken!
Will you rely on your friends?!
Behold, all hands are feeble, and all knees become like water!
Will you trust in your gold and your silver?
They cannot save you!
Will you depend on the formalities and the letter of worship!
Your God asks for the heart and the depths!
Will you lean on authority?!
Behold, everything passes away!
How long will you wait, O my soul?!

entries.section: 1. The personal iniquity of the enquirer:

paragraphs.text: 1 Then came certain of the elders of Israel unto me, and sat before me. 2 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 3 "Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face: should I be enquired of at all by them? 4 Therefore speak unto them, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Every man of the house of Israel that setteth up his idols in his heart, and putteth the stumblingblock of his iniquity before his face, and cometh to the prophet; I the LORD will answer him that cometh according to the multitude of his idols; 5 That I may take the house of Israel in their own heart, because they are all estranged from me through their idols. 6 Therefore say unto the house of Israel, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Repent, and turn yourselves from your idols; and turn away your faces from all your abominations. 7 For every one of the house of Israel, or of the stranger that sojourneth in Israel, which separateth himself from me, and setteth up his idols in his heart, and putteth the stumblingblock of his iniquity before his face, and cometh to a prophet to enquire of him concerning me; I the LORD will answer him by myself: 8 And I will set my face against that man, and will make him a sign and a proverb, and I will cut him off from the midst of my people; and ye shall know that I am the LORD."

entries.section: 1. The personal iniquity of the enquirer:

paragraphs.text: When men from the elders of Israel came and sat before him to enquire, the word of the Lord came to him: "Son of man, these men have set up their idols in their heart, and put the stumblingblock of their iniquity before their face: should I be enquired of at all by them?" [3]. Truly they came to ask God, not the idols, asking Him through Ezekiel himself, the true prophet. But how can God answer the question of one who has worshipped idols in his heart? Their unseen iniquity became a stumblingblock that shut the door of God's answer in their faces. He answers not according to the heart of the prophet but according to the multitude of their idols, which have taken possession of their hearts [4-5].

entries.section: 1. The personal iniquity of the enquirer:

paragraphs.text: He withheld His answer from them in order to stir up in them the spirit of repentance... "Repent, and turn yourselves from your idols; and turn away your faces from all your abominations" [6]. He speaks to them with complete frankness: He will not answer them until they drive their idols out of their hearts, so that the Lord Himself may again reign in the heart.

entries.section: 2. The personal iniquity of the prophet:

paragraphs.text: 9 And if the prophet be deceived when he hath spoken a thing, I the LORD have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. 10 And they shall bear the punishment of their iniquity: the punishment of the prophet shall be even as the punishment of him that seeketh unto him; 11 That the house of Israel may go no more astray from me, neither be polluted any more with all their transgressions; but that they may be my people, and I may be their God, saith the Lord GOD."

"And if the prophet be deceived when he hath spoken a thing, I the LORD have deceived that prophet, and I will stretch out my hand upon him, and will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel. And they shall bear the punishment of their iniquity: the punishment of the prophet shall be even as the punishment of him that seeketh unto him" [9-10]. I show no partiality: if the enquirer sins, I repay him according to his wicked heart, and if the prophet sins, I repay him according to his heart. God judges the priest as He judges the people, the servant as those he serves.

entries.section: 3. Man's accountability for his own conduct:

paragraphs.text: 12 The word of the LORD came again to me, saying, 13 "Son of man, when the land sinneth against me by trespassing grievously, then will I stretch out mine hand upon it, and will break the staff of the bread thereof, and will send famine upon it, and will cut off man and beast from it: 14 Though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord GOD. 15 If I cause noisome beasts to pass through the land, and they spoil it, so that it be desolate, that no man may pass through because of the beasts: 16 Though these three men were in it, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters; they only shall be delivered, but the land shall be desolate. 17 Or if I bring a sword upon that land, and say, Sword, go through the land; so that I cut off man and beast from it: 18 Though these three men were in it, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, they shall deliver neither sons nor daughters, but they only shall be delivered themselves. 19 Or if I send a pestilence into that land, and pour out my fury upon it in blood, to cut off from it man and beast: 20 Though Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, as I live, saith the Lord GOD, they shall deliver neither son nor daughter; they shall but deliver their own souls by their righteousness."

entries.section: 3. Man's accountability for his own conduct:

paragraphs.text: The word of God came to him: "Son of man, when the land sinneth against me by trespassing grievously, then will I stretch out mine hand upon it, and will break the staff of the bread thereof, and will send famine upon it, and will cut off man and beast from it: though these three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job, were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness, saith the Lord GOD" [13-14].
He says, "when the land sinneth against me"; what does he mean by the land?
a. Origen sees that it does not mean the inhabitants of the land.

b. In his view every sinner is counted as earth: [The sinner is called earth, because it was said to Adam: "Thou art earth, and unto earth shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19). Thus we can say that the commission of sin makes the sinner earth... When the earth beholds God, it trembles and is troubled... and we also, like the earth, tremble and are troubled because of our sins].

The Lord affirmed that if the land sinned and betrayed Him, and He struck it with famine, and these three, "Noah, Daniel, and Job," were in it, they would not deliver anyone, but their own souls would be delivered by their righteousness. Then He affirmed again that if the land were struck with noisome, ravening beasts which bereaved its inhabitants, these men would deliver neither sons nor daughters. A third time, if the Lord brought a sword to cut off man and beast from the land, these three would not deliver sons or daughters. And finally, a fourth time, if He brought a pestilence upon the land and poured out His fury upon it in blood, these would deliver neither son nor daughter, but would deliver their own souls by their righteousness. It is as though the Lord, in the Book of Ezekiel, were constantly affirming man's personal responsibility for his faith and his life: we have seen the enquirer (the people) bearing his own iniquity, and the prophet also, and here He affirms that if He finds a righteous man, that man is saved, but he cannot rescue even his son or daughter if the children do not walk in righteousness like their fathers. If this generation is of the seed of Abraham, the father of the fathers and the man of faith, that profits them nothing; and if the generation before them turned aside to idol worship, that does not bind them to the divine wrath, but they are called to account for themselves... This is what He will affirm again, more clearly, in chapter eighteen.

In the light of this chapter we understand the role of the saints in our life, as St. John Chrysostom says: [If we are negligent, we cannot obtain our salvation, not even by the help of others... I say this not to set aside the petitions of the saints, but to put an end to your negligence and to your contentment with relying on others while you lie flat on your backs], and he also says: [How great are the blessings of the prayers of the saints, if we also are working].

Intercession for the people was a living part of the work of the prophets and priests. The prophet Samuel says: "Moreover as for me, God forbid that I should sin against the LORD in ceasing to pray for you" (1 Sam 12:23). And at Mizpeh, when the Philistines rose up against them, they said to Samuel: "Cease not to cry unto the LORD our God for us, that he will save us out of the hand of the Philistines" (1 Sam 7:8). Moses also interceded for his people, until the Lord said to him: "Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation" (Ex 32:10)... The prayers of the saints support the striving soul that desires repentance, but if it persists in its stubbornness they avail it nothing, for the Lord says to the prophet Jeremiah: "Therefore pray not thou for this people, neither lift up cry nor prayer for them, neither make intercession to me: for I will not hear thee" (Jer 7:16; 11:14). God, who said, "For I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake" (2 Kgs 19:14), in the days of Hezekiah the righteous king, did not say this in the days of abounding evil, when He delivered the city to Nebuchadnezzar.

entries.section: Why did He choose these men: Noah, Daniel and Job?

paragraphs.text: Perhaps because they represent a sample of righteous men who lived in the midst of the wicked: Noah lived among a corrupt generation that deserved the flood, and Job kept his righteousness in a pagan environment. As for Daniel, either the Daniel who lived with the three young men in the land of captivity, pure, far from every possibility of a holy life, is meant, or perhaps the Daniel mentioned in the tablets of Ras-shamra, which go back to about 1400 B.C., a wise man and a Phoenician judge, who judged justly in the cases of widows and orphans. In this way the Lord rebuked this Jewish people, for He presented three righteous men who were not Hebrews: Noah and Job, who lived before Abraham, and Daniel, a Phoenician man, as though God were affirming to them that He shows no partiality. He desires the salvation of every soul, whatever its race, as long as it responds to His love and His commandment.
St. Augustine sees that these men represent types, for he says: [In these three men God undoubtedly presented types of the three ranks of men who are saved].

I believe that Noah represents the righteous leaders of the nations, because of his ordering of the flood as a type of the Church, Daniel represents the righteous in purity, and Job represents the righteous who are married.

Origen sees that each of the three passed through three stages: a period of happiness followed by a stage of sorrow and pain, then a return to joy and happiness. Thus a man begins his spiritual life with divine consolations, followed by a narrow way and troubles that bring him into new spiritual glories... This is the way of the glorified Cross, or the way of fellowship with the suffering Christ who rose from the dead, or the way of salvation.
The bitter punishments under which man falls because of his sins are four:
a. Famine, which cuts off man and beast from the land [13].

entries.section: Why did He choose these men: Noah, Daniel and Job?

paragraphs.text: b. Noisome beasts, which turn the land into a desolation and bereave mothers [15].

entries.section: Why did He choose these men: Noah, Daniel and Job?

paragraphs.text: c. The sword, which cuts off man and beast from the land [17].

entries.section: Why did He choose these men: Noah, Daniel and Job?

paragraphs.text: d. The pestilence, which pours out God's fury upon the land in blood [19].

As for His mention of "man and beast," it is because man points to the rational or soul side, and the beast to the bodily side; as though sin, which deprives man of God, causes him to lose both the spiritual and the temporal blessings, or the blessings of the inner soul and also of the body.

Hunger, the loss of security (the noisome beasts), the removal of peace (the sword), and the deprivation of health (the pestilence) are the natural fruits that man gathers from sin, which isolates him from God, the source of his satisfaction, security, peace and health. Therefore, when St. Augustine feels hunger and anxiety he takes refuge in God, addressing Him:
[My God... You have made my soul able to contain Your infinite majesty, lest it have anything that is able to fill it besides You!
My God... You have made us for Yourself... therefore our heart remains troubled, anxious, and without rest at all times until it rests in You].

These strokes, with the types they carry, represent four aspects resulting from the work of sin in man's life: famine, because of the loss of the knowledge of the truth; the noisome beasts, which represent the domination of the demons over the soul, so that they kill every virtue in it and make the soul like a bereaved mother without hope; the sword, in that man loses his vitality and becomes like one slain, of no use; and finally the pestilence, in that man becomes a germ of corruption that destroys those around him. It is as though the strokes signify man's deprivation of the truth and his subjection to the domination of the devil, his deprivation of all vitality and his becoming a focus of corruption for others!

entries.section: 4. God's care for the repentant remnant:

paragraphs.text: 21 "For thus saith the Lord GOD; How much more when I send my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast? 22 Yet, behold, therein shall be left a remnant that shall be brought forth, both sons and daughters: behold, they shall come forth unto you, and ye shall see their way and their doings: and ye shall be comforted concerning the evil that I have brought upon Jerusalem, even concerning all that I have brought upon it. 23 And they shall comfort you, when ye see their ways and their doings: and ye shall know that I have not done without cause all that I have done in it, saith the Lord GOD."
Every time God speaks of the chastening of His people or of His wrath because of their multiplied sins, He does not forget to affirm His care for the small repentant remnant.
I have sinned! I have sinned!
* My God... how hard it is for my soul to confess!
Reveal to me my hidden depths, that I may cry out:
I have sinned! I have sinned!
* In former times the people laid the blame on the priests, and the priests laid the blame on the people, and every generation thought that it was being punished for the faults of its fathers.
But I confess to You:
I have sinned! I have sinned!
* My father will not intercede for me if I neglect my salvation!
And I will not be punished for his weaknesses!
I confess to You my personal responsibility!
I have sinned, so pardon me and forgive me!
* The prophet Moses interceded for his people, and the prophet Samuel did not cease to pray for them; we are surrounded by a cloud of witnesses, who intercede and pray for us and support us!
Teach me to care for the salvation of my soul, so that the cloud may truly be a support to me!
* I complain to You of my soul, for sin has shattered me:
A famine of the word of the Lord has come upon me!
I have become a wilderness, in which evil thoughts dwell like noisome beasts!
The sword of sin has struck my depths, shattering my powers!
By my sin I have become like a corrupting pestilence to those around me.
I confess my sin to You, for I alone am the debtor!
Save me... rescue me!

1 And the word of the LORD came unto me, saying, 2 "Son of man, What is the vine tree more than any tree, or than a branch which is among the trees of the forest? 3 Shall wood be taken thereof to do any work? or will men take a pin of it to hang any vessel thereon? 4 Behold, it is cast into the fire for fuel; the fire devoureth both the ends of it, and the midst of it is burned. Is it meet for any work? 5 Behold, when it was whole, it was meet for no work: how much less shall it be meet yet for any work, when the fire hath devoured it, and it is burned? 6 Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; As the vine tree among the trees of the forest, which I have given to the fire for fuel, so will I give the inhabitants of Jerusalem. 7 And I will set my face against them; they shall go out from one fire, and another fire shall devour them; and ye shall know that I am the LORD, when I set my face against them. 8 And I will make the land desolate, because they have committed a trespass, saith the Lord GOD."

God often addresses His people as His divine vineyard, which He planted with His right hand and tended Himself, and which He never left in want of anything. God chose the vine because among the other trees it is considered small, with pliant wood... its wood is not fit as planks for building purposes, nor as cords and supports for tents, nor even as fuel, for the fire devours it entirely in moments... Almost its only distinction is its abundant fruit. If it does not bear fruit, it is good for nothing at all. So it is with what God requires of His Church: the precious fruit of the Spirit.

In the prophet Isaiah He declares that He set it on a fruitful hill, He fenced it and gathered out the stones thereof, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein (Isa 5:1-2). He gave it every possibility of bearing fruit: He hedged it about with His Holy Spirit, took away from it the stony nature, and gave it the tower of divine knowledge... and He looked for good fruit, and behold, it brought forth wild grapes. Therefore He punishes it, saying: "And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, and men of Judah, judge, I pray you, betwixt me and my vineyard. What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes? And now go to; I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard: I will take away the hedge thereof, and it shall be eaten up; and break down the wall thereof, and it shall be trodden down: And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold a cry" (Isa 5:3-7).

Again the Psalmist describes the people of God as the vine of the Lord, which He tended with His right hand, but which did not keep its being... for he says: "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land. The hills were covered with the shadow of it, and the boughs thereof were like the goodly cedars. She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river. Why hast thou then broken down her hedges, so that all they which pass by the way do pluck her? The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it" (Ps 80:8-13).

This is what happened literally to the people of Israel, as it happens symbolically in the life of many. Literally, the Lord established His people in Egypt as the first plant, on the level of a nation of His own, then transplanted it from there by the hand of Moses, with a high hand and a strong arm. He drove out many nations from before its face that it might dwell in the Promised Land, so its people multiplied and increased in number and filled the Promised Land, and embraced the mountains of Israel and the cedars of Lebanon, extending east of the Mediterranean to the river Jordan... But when it turned away from God, the Lord broke down its wall, and many strangers entered it and humbled it, and it became unclean by the entry of idolatrous worship into its temple, and instead of the Lord's care for it, the wild beast within it came to devour its children.

Symbolically, however, the believer, planted in Egypt (the world), is brought by the Lord across to the heavenly Jerusalem, and is led into the heavenly places by the hand of the Lord Christ Himself with a strong hand. He drives out from before him all the powers of darkness, so that they have no place in his heart, and he lives as a king, having authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, embracing within himself the holy mountains (the prophets of the Old Testament and the apostles of the New Testament) and the cedars of God, as he enters into fellowship with the saints who live in the uprightness of the cedar. His life extends to the sea and the river, that is, to the streams of holy waters, or the blessed river of Baptism, that it may live by the Holy Spirit of God as the secret of its enlightenment and its constant growth. Such a soul, if it does not stand firm in what has been given it to the end, is lost and becomes the plaything of Satan! Therefore the Apostle Paul warns us: "Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall" (1 Cor 10:12).

entries.section: The vine tree:

paragraphs.text: If the Church of the Old Testament, like that of the New Testament, was called a vine among the trees of the forest, because it bore the cluster of life, the Lord of glory Jesus, who is the secret of our joy and exultation, and bore fruit among the unfruitful trees of the forest, then in this chapter the ancient people is called the vine tree more than any tree, or than the branch which is among the trees of the forest. It is the branch of the vine which was required to bear the cluster, but alas, being cut off from the root, it became dry and useless. It dried up, and the fire devoured both its ends and burned its midst; is it meet for any work? "Behold, when it was whole, it was meet for no work: how much less shall it be meet yet for any work, when the fire hath devoured it, and it is burned?" [5].

First: it was cut off from the root, so it lost its life and was no longer fit for anything but to be burned with the fire of judgment, and as St. Augustine says: [The branch suits only one of two things: either the vine or the fire. If it does not abide in the vine, its portion is the fire. And if it wishes to escape the latter place, it must have its place in the vine].

Second: the burning of its two ends is a reference to what befell this people because of their sins, for the northern kingdom fell in 721 B.C. in the Assyrian captivity, and the southern kingdom in its first captivity, about 597 B.C. What befell it, its withdrawal from God Himself, was an inner burning because of sin. Therefore the total burning must needs come.
Make me abide in You, O true Vine!
* Make me abide in You, O true Vine, for without You I wither and am not fit even for the burning!
* Behold, I am a bruised reed; do not break me!
Mend my state with the touches of Your healing hand!
Grant me Your Holy Spirit working in me!
Instead of dryness let me bear living fruits, and instead of death let me breathe eternal life!
* You watered Your vineyard with Your precious blood; You planted Your Church as a good vine, You surrounded it with the walls of Your Holy Spirit, and You gave it every possibility of bearing fruit!
Work, that I may bear Your fruit within me, O Holy One!

entries.section: 1. Personal responsibility:

paragraphs.text: 1 The word of the LORD came unto me again, saying, 2 "What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? 3 As I live, saith the Lord GOD, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. 4 Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die. 5 But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right, 6 And hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, neither hath defiled his neighbour's wife, neither hath come near to a menstruous woman, 7 And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment; 8 He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man, 9 Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live, saith the Lord GOD.

entries.section: 1. Personal responsibility:

paragraphs.text: In this chapter the Lord dealt with the proverb that was common among the Jewish people: "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" [2]. They felt that the divine wrath that came upon them was only the fruit of the evil of their fathers, who had brought idol worship into the divine sanctuaries. But the Lord wanted to affirm that He will not recompense a man for the sins of his parents, and that the discipline He permits is because of what people do in their own time.

We dealt with this subject earlier, in the commentary on the Book of Exodus, where the Lord says, "For I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5). We saw that God does not mean by this that He makes one generation bear the sins of the former generations; rather, in His love He is longsuffering toward one generation and a second, that perhaps they may repent. If they do not repent, He makes the third generation, and the fourth as well, bear the discipline, because they did not repent through their fathers, since He calls them "them that hate me." But if they repent through their fathers, they are not counted as sons of the wicked; rather God Himself becomes their Father, and they enjoy His grace.
* The soul that does not dwell in God is the source of its own evils, so it sins, and the soul that sins is the one that dies.

entries.section: 1. Personal responsibility:

paragraphs.text: St. Ambrose: There is no partiality with God; the soul of the father is as the soul of the son, or as He says: "Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die" [4]... Here we ask:
First: Does a man inherit nothing of the weaknesses of his father?
Second: Does the soul die?

entries.section: First: Does a man inherit nothing of the weaknesses of his father?

paragraphs.text: The Holy Bible does not ignore the effect of parents on a person's life. A person who is born in a holy home and brought up between godly parents finds a possibility that helps the growth of his spiritual life and the setting out of his soul to live with God. On the contrary, if he has a wicked father and a wicked mother, then even if they do not encourage their son to sin and evil, at the very least they stand as a stumbling block before his spiritual growth. Nevertheless, many children loved evil in spite of the godliness of their parents, such as the two sons of Eli the priest, and there are also children who loved righteousness in spite of the evil of their fathers. The environment in which a person lives may be good or evil, but it does not compel him to goodness or evil. Indeed, a man himself may begin his life with evil and then return and complete his way with God, and he may begin in the Spirit and then fall back into evil and live in sin. For this reason this chapter has presented to us four examples: one who was wicked though his father was righteous, one who was righteous though his father was wicked, and one who was righteous and then turned aside, or the opposite. This happened in the kings of Judah. Hezekiah the good king was a consecrated servant, who "did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done" (2 Chr 29:2); he opened his reign by repairing and cleansing the Temple, removed the high places and cast out the images... But his father Ahaz had his heart attached to the love of idols from the beginning of his reign, made his son pass through the fire and sacrificed on the high places (2 Kgs 16:3-4); indeed he shut up the doors of the porch of the Temple, put out the lamps, and burned no incense nor offered burnt offerings to the living God (2 Chr 29:7). As for Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, he led his people astray from the truth, and made them sacrifice to all the host of heaven, and they did worse than the nations whom the LORD had destroyed before the children of Israel (2 Kgs 21:2-9), although in the last of his days he amended much of what he had corrupted (2 Chr 33:1-20).

entries.section: Second: Does the soul die?

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome distinguishes between the saying of the Psalmist: "What man is he that liveth, and shall not see death?" (Ps 89:48), and what is said by Ezekiel the prophet: "The soul that sinneth, it shall die" [4], saying: [There is a difference between seeing death and tasting it, for he who sees, sees indeed but does not taste it, while he who tastes it of necessity sees it]. By this he means that all mankind sees death, the death of the body, but he whose soul is sanctified in the Lord sees the death of his body yet does not taste death, since he bears the power of Christ's resurrection working in him.

* As there is a death of the body, there is a death of the soul... The death of the soul is in any case not like the death of the body; it is utterly dreadful. The death of the body is the separation of the soul from the body, the one from the other, so that man is released from pending cares and toils, and the other (the soul) is transferred to a clear dwelling. Then, when the body is dissolved and decomposes, it is gathered together again in incorruption and receives its soul back again. This is the death of the body, but the death of the soul is fearful and terrifying. In it, when dissolution takes place, the soul does not come to an end as the body does, but is joined to the body again and is not annihilated; it is cast with it into the fire that is not quenched.
St. John Chrysostom: * This death (of the soul) has as its opponent and enemy Him who said: "I am the life" (Jn 14:6).
Origen: * According to the Holy Scriptures we learn that there are three kinds of death:

A death when we die to sin and live to God. Blessed is this death by which we flee from sin and are consecrated to God, for it separates us from what is mortal and sanctifies us to Him who is immortal.
The other death is the departure from this life, as the father Abraham and the father David died and were buried with their fathers, when the soul is freed from the bonds of the body.

The third death is that of which it was said, "Let the dead bury their dead" (Mt 8:22). By this death not only the body dies but the soul also, for "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:4); it dies to the Lord, not through the weakness of nature but through the weakness of committing transgression. This death is not a leaving of this life but a falling into error.
Therefore spiritual death is one thing, natural death another, and the third is death as punishment.

St. Ambrose: St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the words found in this chapter [4-9] "contain a description of the conduct of Christians, in which God nobly urges us to the blessed life, which is the reward of a life of goodness, eternal life." This description includes the positive and negative aspects in the life of the believer:

entries.section: Second: Does the soul die?

paragraphs.text: A. It befits the Christian to walk in righteousness, to do that which is lawful and right [5], not to eat upon the mountains that were defiled by the sacrifices of the idolaters, nor to lift up his eyes to their idols. Thus he is sanctified entirely: he is sanctified in his heart by righteousness, truth and justice, and sanctified in his eating by refraining from taking part in pagan feasts, and sanctified even in the glances of his eyes, so that he does not lift up his eyes to their idols. He is sanctified by the positive work, which is doing righteousness and loving truth and justice, and negatively by refraining from everything that is evil...

B. The Christian does not defile his neighbour's wife, nor does he come near his own wife when she is menstruous; he loves holiness in his inner life and in his body as in others; he does not covet his brother's wife...

entries.section: Second: Does the soul die?

paragraphs.text: C. He does not practice injustice against anyone, not only by giving others their lawful rights, but he gives the poor man his right in sharing his needs, and gives the naked man his right in sharing his clothes with him, and offers the needy debtor the right of love and mercy, so that he demands no usury from him, and he offers others the right of supporting the wronged against the wrongdoer, so that he does not stand by passively but "hath executed true judgment between man and man" [8].

entries.section: Second: Does the soul die?

paragraphs.text: D. The secret of his righteous life is his entering into the divine commandment, as the Lord says: "Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just" [9].

entries.section: 2. A wicked son of a righteous father:

paragraphs.text: 10 "If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, and that doeth the like to any one of these things, 11 And that doeth not any of those duties, but even hath eaten upon the mountains, and defiled his neighbour's wife, 12 Hath oppressed the poor and needy, hath spoiled by violence, hath not restored the pledge, and hath lifted up his eyes to the idols, hath committed abomination, 13 Hath given forth upon usury, and hath taken increase: shall he then live? he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him.

entries.section: 2. A wicked son of a righteous father:

paragraphs.text: The first example the Lord gave concerning personal responsibility is the wicked son of the righteous father. He "shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him" [13]. His father's righteousness does not rescue him from the fruit of his abominations, but he shall surely die.

St. Jerome wrote to the deacon Sabinianus, urging him to repent, as follows: [Perhaps you are deluded in yourself that the bishop who ordained you is a holy man, and you think that his merits atone for your transgressions. I have already told you that the father is not punished for his son, nor the son for his father. The soul that sinneth, it shall die].

entries.section: 3. A righteous son of a wicked father:

paragraphs.text: 14 "Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like, 15 That hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, hath not defiled his neighbour's wife, 16 Neither hath oppressed any, hath not withholden the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment, 17 That hath taken off his hand from the poor, that hath not received usury nor increase, hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes; he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. 18 As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity. 19 Yet say ye, Why? doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father? When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live. 20 The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.

The people in the days of King Zedekiah thought that they were more righteous than the people in the days of King Manasseh, so they felt that they were bearing the iniquity of their fathers. But the Lord affirms here: "If he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like... he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity" [14-19].
When a man commits iniquity he loses his life, as St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [Sin is nothing but estrangement from God, who alone is the true life].

But perhaps some will ask: How does the righteous son not bear the iniquity of his father when it has been said: "Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered with the LORD; and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out" (Ps 109:14)?

St. Augustine answers: [Is it to be understood that even the iniquity of his fathers comes upon a man? Those who are converted in Christ do not have the iniquity of their fathers come upon them, since they are no longer sons of the wicked, because they did not imitate their conduct. Therefore it is added to the words: "visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children... of them that hate me" (Ex 20:5), that is, those who hate me as their fathers hated me].

entries.section: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

paragraphs.text: 21 "But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 22 All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live. 23 Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? 24 But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die. 25 Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal? 26 When a righteous man turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and dieth in them; for his iniquity that he hath done shall he die. 27 Again, when the wicked man turneth away from his wickedness that he hath committed, and doeth that which is lawful and right, he shall save his soul alive. 28 Because he considereth, and turneth away from all his transgressions that he hath committed, he shall surely live, he shall not die. 29 Yet saith the house of Israel, The way of the Lord is not equal. O house of Israel, are not my ways equal? are not your ways unequal? 30 Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord GOD. Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. 31 Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel? 32 For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.

We have said that the Lord wanted by His speech here to move His people toward repentance, that they should not be troubled because of the sins of their fathers, and also that they should not be troubled by their own previous or present personal sins if they offer true repentance, for He says: "If the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die" [21]. Some consider this statement the center of the whole book, the most precious statement found in it; it is a powerful call to repentance! "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" [23]. He opens the door of hope wide, so that not one soul may perish in a spirit of deadly despair.

The Fathers of the Church found in this chapter a fertile field into which every fallen, despairing person may enter to eat of the fruit of repentance and be filled with hope, while it also gives clear warnings to the souls that stand, lest by their negligence they lose all their past labor. The following are some comments of the Fathers:
* By encouragement He lightens the weight of sins and lessens the passions, inspiring hope of salvation.

St. Clement of Alexandria: * For those who are in danger of despair He provided the refuge of forgiveness, and for those who are in danger of (presumptuous) hope, who delay by putting off, He made the day of death uncertain.
St. Augustine: * If they hear this voice and believe it, they will be healed of despair and rise from the bottomless pit of depths into which they have fallen.
St. Augustine: * We do not despair of any man as long as God's longsuffering leads the wicked to repentance, so we do not drive him out of this life.

St. Augustine: * Do not despair of salvation. Remember what is written in the Holy Scripture, that he who falls arises and he who strays returns (Jer 8:4), and the wounded is healed, and he who fell prey to the beasts escapes, and he who confesses his sins is not despised... It is a time for endurance and longsuffering, a time for healing and correction. Have you stumbled? Arise! Have you sinned? Cease from sin!
St. Augustine: * Repentance is a "life" better than death...
Hasten to it, O sinner, and embrace it as a drowning man embraces some planks, so that it may snatch you from drowning amid the waves of sins and carry you to the divine harbor, full of tenderness.
Tertullian: * Since what the Lord says is true, when I repent He forgets all my past sins and all my iniquities; why do you frighten me?
God promises me forgiveness; would you cast me into despair?

entries.section: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

paragraphs.text: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: At the very time when He opens the doors of hope with all power before sinners that they may repent, He warns those who stand lest they fall, saying: "But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die" [24]. And as St. Anba Anthony says: [Let us persevere in our training every day, knowing that if we neglect it for one single day the Lord will not forgive us for the sake of the past, but will bring His wrath upon our negligence... for Judas ruined his past striving because of one night].

And St. Basil the Great says: [When a change occurs, the labor of the righteous becomes vain, just as the sinner is not blamed, by the first turning away from what is good to what is worse, and the second inclining from what is evil to what is better].

But is not this statement harsh and severe? St. John Chrysostom answers: [Even in this matter God showed the greatness of the tenderness of His love, presenting to us these terrifying things in order to raise us up and awaken in us a desire for the Kingdom]. And St. Clement of Alexandria says: [The punishments of God are for salvation, and discipline leads us to repentance, for God longs for repentance more than for the death of the sinner].

entries.section: 4. A man's turning from his evil:

paragraphs.text: "For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord GOD: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye" [32].
God speaks these words to you if you are wretched: "For I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked."
Even if you want your own death, I do not want it.
You did not create yourself, but by despair you perish.
In any case, God created you when you did not exist; afterward He sought you when you went astray, and found you through the blood of His Son and saved you.
He Himself calls you: Return from the abyss of despair. Come, for I do not desire the death of the sinner but that he return and live...
Do not lose confidence through despair about your sins, and at the same time do not trust in length of life. Therefore repent... Why do you not repent today?

Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: Origen sees in this divine speech concerning the possibility of sinners' returning to God and the warning of those who stand against falling, a confirmation of the error of those who say that there are different natures created thus, showing that the sinner can become good and the opposite.
You did not create me to die!
* You created me to live in the world as a king, in my royal palace!
You did not create me to die, but to live by You and with You!
* You are wonderful, O Lord, in Your love for me, for even if I seek death, You desire my life!
I do not know what is for my edification and my glory!
But You know all that is for my life, O my Creator!
* You do not will my death but my life; You do not hold me accountable for the errors of my fathers, nor wound my feelings for sins I have left behind. You are wonderful in Your care for me!
* You are the Savior of souls from corruption; You alone are able to renew my nature, O my Savior!
